claim: Teeth are present in most clades of vertebrates but have been lost completely several times in actinopterygian fishes and amniotes.
source: Teeth are present in most clades of vertebrates but have been lost completely several times in actinopterygian fishes and amniotes.
evidence: This is a general statement about vertebrate tooth evolution supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Dentition is invariably present in caecilians and salamanders.
source: We demonstrate that dentition is invariably present in caecilians and salamanders
evidence: Based on microCT data collected from 65 salamander and 30 caecilian species showing all examined specimens have teeth.

claim: Teeth have been lost completely more than 20 times in frogs.
source: teeth have been lost completely more than 20 times in frogs
evidence: Based on ancestral state reconstruction analysis using reversible-jump MCMC in RevBayes on 524 amphibian species.

claim: Frogs have a much higher occurrence of edentulism than any other vertebrate group.
source: a much higher occurrence of edentulism than in any other vertebrate group
evidence: Comparative analysis showing at least 22 independent origins of edentulism in frogs versus only 8 other edentulous vertebrate lineages identified in literature review.

claim: The repeated loss of teeth in anurans is associated with a specialized diet of small invertebrate prey.
source: The repeated loss of teeth in anurans is associated with a specialized diet of small invertebrate prey
evidence: BayesTrait discrete analysis showing correlated evolution between edentulism and microphagy with Bayes factor = 54.32.

claim: The repeated loss of teeth in anurans is associated with shortening of the lower jaw.
source: The repeated loss of teeth in anurans is associated with a specialized diet of small invertebrate prey as well as shortening of the lower jaw
evidence: Phylogenetic logistic regression showing significant relationship between edentulism and shortened jaws (p<0.001) in 423 anuran species.

claim: The repeated loss of teeth in anurans is not correlated with a reduction in body size.
source: but it is not correlated with a reduction in body size
evidence: Phylogenetic logistic regression showing no relationship between edentulism and body size (p=0.09) in 423 anuran species.

claim: The evolution of teeth is considered a key innovation that promoted the radiation of jawed vertebrates.
source: The evolution of teeth is considered a key innovation that promoted the radiation of jawed vertebrates, facilitating the transition from a passive to active predatory lifestyle (Gans and Northcutt, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gans and Northcutt, 1983.

claim: Teeth originated in stem gnathostomes more than 400 million years ago.
source: Teeth are complex mineralized tissues that originated in stem gnathostomes more than 400 million years ago (Rücklin et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rücklin et al., 2012.

claim: Teeth have been lost completely in three extant clades of mammals (baleen whales, anteaters, and pangolins), turtles, and birds.
source: teeth have been lost completely several times, resulting in toothlessness or edentulism, including in three extant clades of mammals (baleen whales, anteaters, and pangolins), turtles, and birds (Davit-Béal et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davit-Béal et al., 2009.

claim: Teeth are likely lost following the evolution of a secondary feeding tool that improves the efficiency of food intake.
source: Teeth are likely lost following the evolution of a secondary feeding tool that improves the efficiency of food intake (e.g., beak, baleen, specialized tongue), leading to relaxed functional constraints on dentition (Davit-Béal et al., 2009).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citation to Davit-Béal et al., 2009.

claim: All living salamanders and caecilians are assumed to have teeth on the upper jaw, lower jaw, and palate.
source: All living salamanders and caecilians are assumed to have teeth on the upper jaw, lower jaw, and palate (Duellman and Trueb, 1986)
evidence: Supported by citation to Duellman and Trueb, 1986.

claim: Nearly all frogs lack dentition on the lower jaw and variably possess teeth on the upper jaw and palate.
source: but nearly all frogs lack dentition on the lower jaw and variably possess teeth on the upper jaw and palate
evidence: Based on established knowledge and confirmed by microCT data from 429 frog species.

claim: Amphibian teeth are typically pedicellate, bicuspid, homodont, and continuously replaced.
source: When present, amphibian teeth are typically pedicellate (each tooth consists of a crown and pedicel separated by a noncalcified dividing zone), bicuspid, homodont, and continuously replaced (Davit-Béal et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davit-Béal et al., 2007.

claim: Dentition on the lower jaw was lost in the ancestor of frogs more than 200 million years ago.
source: Recent work suggests that dentition on the lower jaw was lost in the ancestor of frogs more than 200 million years ago and was subsequently regained in a single species (Gastrotheca guentheri; Boulenger, 1882) during the Miocene (Wiens, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wiens, 2011.

claim: Dentition on the lower jaw was subsequently regained in a single species (Gastrotheca guentheri) during the Miocene.
source: Recent work suggests that dentition on the lower jaw was lost in the ancestor of frogs more than 200 million years ago and was subsequently regained in a single species (Gastrotheca guentheri; Boulenger, 1882) during the Miocene (Wiens, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wiens, 2011.

claim: Most frogs are generalist, gape-limited predators that capture prey using tongue propulsion.
source: Most frogs are generalist, gape-limited predators that capture prey using tongue propulsion (Regal and Gans, 1976)
evidence: Supported by citation to Regal and Gans, 1976.

claim: Tooth loss is hypothesized to occur in frogs that specialize on eating small prey (microphagy), such as ants and termites.
source: Tooth loss is hypothesized to occur in frogs that specialize on eating small prey (microphagy), such as ants and termites (Das and Coe, 1994; Parmelee, 1999; Narváez and Ron, 2013).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations to Das and Coe, 1994; Parmelee, 1999; Narváez and Ron, 2013.

claim: Microphagous frogs are known to have shortened jaws and altered feeding cycles.
source: Microphagous frogs are known to have shortened jaws and altered feeding cycles (Emerson, 1985)
evidence: Supported by citation to Emerson, 1985.

claim: Microphagous frogs have modified tongues.
source: modified tongues (Trueb and Gans, 1983)
evidence: Supported by citation to Trueb and Gans, 1983.

claim: Some microphagous frogs have the ability to sequester dietary alkaloids from their prey, rendering them toxic.
source: and some have the ability to sequester dietary alkaloids from their prey, rendering them toxic (Caldwell, 1996; Vences et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caldwell, 1996; Vences et al., 1998.

claim: Teeth may be reduced or lost as a byproduct of miniaturization or truncated development (paedomorphosis).
source: Alternately, teeth may be reduced or lost as a byproduct of miniaturization or truncated development (paedomorphosis; Davies, 1989; Hanken and Wake, 1993; Smirnov and Vasil'eva, 1995)
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations to Davies, 1989; Hanken and Wake, 1993; Smirnov and Vasil'eva, 1995.

claim: The initiation of odontogenesis occurs ontogenetically late in frogs (during or after metamorphosis) compared to other vertebrates.
source: because the initiation of odontogenesis occurs ontogenetically late in frogs (during or after metamorphosis) compared to other vertebrates
evidence: Based on established knowledge of frog development.

claim: Data were collected from high-resolution X-ray micro-computed tomography (microCT) of over 500 of the 562 currently recognized amphibian genera.
source: our extensive taxonomic sampling via high-resolution X-ray micro-computed tomography (microCT) of over 500 of the 562 currently recognized amphibian genera (AmphibiaWeb, 2021)
evidence: Description of data collection methods.

claim: All anuran species lack dentary teeth with the exception of G. guentheri.
source: All anuran species lack dentary teeth with the exception of G. guentheri.
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 429 frog species.

claim: The evolution of maxillary and premaxillary teeth of the upper jaw is synchronized in all frog species.
source: The evolution of maxillary and premaxillary teeth of the upper jaw is synchronized in all frog species (Figure 1A and B), being present in 292 taxa and coordinately absent in 136 species.
evidence: Based on microCT data showing coordinated presence/absence patterns in 429 frog species.

claim: Vomerine teeth on the palate are the most variable in frogs, being present in 202 species and absent in 226.
source: The vomerine teeth on the palate are the most variable in frogs, being present in 202 species and absent in 226.
evidence: Based on microCT data from 429 frog species.

claim: Many anurans have maxillary and premaxillary teeth in the absence of vomerine teeth (92 species).
source: Many anurans have maxillary and premaxillary teeth in the absence of vomerine teeth (92 species)
evidence: Based on microCT data from 429 frog species.

claim: Only two species examined have vomerine teeth while lacking upper jaw teeth (Rhombophryne testudo, Uperodon systoma).
source: but only two species examined have vomerine teeth while lacking upper jaw teeth (Rhombophryne testudo, Uperodon systoma).
evidence: Based on microCT data from 429 frog species.

claim: All 65 salamander species examined have teeth on the lower jaw and palate.
source: All 65 salamander species examined have teeth on the lower jaw and palate
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 65 salamander species.

claim: Three salamander species lack upper jaw teeth on the maxilla and premaxilla (the sirenids Siren intermedia and Pseudobranchus striatus and the salamandrid Salamandrina terdigitata).
source: but three species lack upper jaw teeth on the maxilla and premaxilla (the sirenids Siren intermedia and Pseudobranchus striatus and the salamandrid Salamandrina terdigitata).
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 65 salamander species.

claim: Thorius pennatulus and two proteids (Necturus lewisi and Proteus anguinus) lack maxillary teeth but retain premaxillary teeth.
source: Thorius pennatulus (Plethodonidae) and two proteids (Necturus lewisi and Proteus anguinus) lack maxillary teeth but retain premaxillary teeth.
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 65 salamander species.

claim: All salamanders have vomerine teeth on the palate.
source: All salamanders have vomerine teeth on the palate (including the paravomerine tooth patches that underlie the parasphenoid in plethodontids; Figure 1C; Lawson et al., 1971).
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 65 salamander species and citation to Lawson et al., 1971.

claim: All 30 caecilian species examined possess marginal teeth on the lower and upper jaw and palatal teeth on multiple elements.
source: All 30 caecilian species examined possess marginal teeth on the lower and upper jaw and palatal teeth on multiple elements (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 30 caecilian species.

claim: Teeth are absent in 134 anuran genera belonging to 19 families.
source: Teeth are absent in 134 anuran genera belonging to 19 families.
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 429 frog species.

claim: The maximum a posteriori model of dentition evolution was the one-rate model with a posterior probability of 0.91.
source: The maximum a posteriori model of dentition evolution was the one-rate model with a posterior probability of 0.91.
evidence: Result from reversible-jump MCMC analysis in RevBayes.

claim: The model-averaged maximum a posteriori ancestral state of Lissamphibia and Anura is toothed with a posterior probability of 0.99.
source: The model-averaged maximum a posteriori ancestral state of Lissamphibia and Anura is toothed with a posterior probability of 0.99.
evidence: Result from reversible-jump MCMC ancestral state reconstruction in RevBayes.

claim: Teeth have been completely lost at least 22 times in frogs.
source: Teeth have been completely lost at least 22 times in frogs (Figure 2)
evidence: Result from ancestral state reconstruction analysis.

claim: Six reversals from edentulous to toothed upper jaws were inferred.
source: and six reversals from edentulous to toothed upper jaws were inferred
evidence: Result from ancestral state reconstruction analysis.

claim: Edentulism has evolved three times in Archaeobatrachia (in Pipoidea).
source: Edentulism has evolved three times in Archaeobatrachia (in Pipoidea, Feng et al., 2017)
evidence: Result from ancestral state reconstruction analysis with phylogenetic context from Feng et al., 2017.

claim: Edentulism has evolved 19 times in Neobatrachia (10 times in Hyloidea, six times in Ranoidea, twice in Myobatrachidae, and once in Nasikabatrachidae).
source: and 19 times in Neobatrachia (10 times in Hyloidea, six times in Ranoidea, twice in Myobatrachidae, and once in Nasikabatrachidae).
evidence: Result from ancestral state reconstruction analysis.

claim: One reversal was estimated in Myobatrachidae (in Uperoleia mahonyi).
source: One reversal was estimated in Myobatrachidae (in Uperoleia mahonyi; Clulow et al., 2016)
evidence: Result from ancestral state reconstruction analysis with citation to Clulow et al., 2016.

claim: Five reversals were inferred in Microhylidae (in Dyscophus, Uperodon, Anodonthyla, Cophyla, and Rhombophryne + Plethodontohyla).
source: and five reversals were inferred in Microhylidae (in Dyscophus, Uperodon, Anodonthyla, Cophyla, and Rhombophryne + Plethodontohyla).
evidence: Result from ancestral state reconstruction analysis.

claim: The all-rates-different model was the best fit for three dental states evolution in frogs.
source: The all-rates-different model was the best fit (all-rates-different Akaike information criterion (AIC) weight (AICw) = 0.91, equal-rates AICw = 0.00, single-rate ordered AICw = 0.00, symmetric ordered AICw = 0.01, unsymmetric ordered AICw = 0.02, symmetric unordered AICw = 0.06)
evidence: Result from discrete character evolution model comparison using fitMk in phytools.

claim: Vomerine tooth loss does not always precede complete edentulism.
source: indicating that vomerine tooth loss does not always precede complete edentulism (Figure 3).
evidence: Result from discrete character evolution model comparison showing all-rates-different model as best fit.

claim: The number of transitions to edentulism is similar between toothed upper jaws with toothless vomers (13.8) and fully toothed states (10.3).
source: Stochastic character mapping suggests that the number of transitions to edentulism is similar between toothed upper jaws with toothless vomers (13.8) and fully toothed states (10.3).
evidence: Result from stochastic character mapping analysis.

claim: Toothed frogs have lost vomerine teeth an estimated 59 times.
source: Toothed frogs have lost vomerine teeth an estimated 59 times (Figure 3).
evidence: Result from stochastic character mapping analysis.

claim: One gain of vomerine teeth subsequent to a loss was inferred in Phlyctimantis leonardi.
source: One gain of vomerine teeth subsequent to a loss was inferred in Phlyctimantis leonardi.
evidence: Result from stochastic character mapping analysis.

claim: 69 taxa from 20 families were classified as microphagous (defined as >50% of diet by number or volume consisting of ants, termites, or mites).
source: We compiled published diet records for 268 frog lineages and classified 69 taxa from 20 families as microphagous (defined here as >50% of diet by number or volume consisting of ants, termites, or mites)
evidence: Based on compilation of published diet records for 268 frog lineages.

claim: 199 taxa from 47 families were classified as generalist feeders.
source: and 199 taxa from 47 families as generalist feeders (Figure 4; Dataset S2).
evidence: Based on compilation of published diet records for 268 frog lineages.

claim: Of the 69 microphagy specialists, 54 are edentulous and 15 are toothed.
source: Of the 69 microphagy specialists, 54 are edentulous and 15 are toothed.
evidence: Based on combined dentition and diet data for 268 frog lineages.

claim: Of the 199 generalists, 25 are edentulous and 174 are toothed.
source: Of the 199 generalists, 25 are edentulous and 174 are toothed.
evidence: Based on combined dentition and diet data for 268 frog lineages.

claim: The dependent model of trait evolution is strongly supported over the independent model for edentulism and microphagy (Bayes factor = 54.32).
source: A BayesTrait discrete analysis indicated correlated evolution between edentulism and microphagy: the dependent model of trait evolution is strongly supported over the independent model (Bayes factor = 54.32; a Bayes factor >2 implies the evolution of two traits is linked).
evidence: Result from BayesTrait discrete analysis on 268 taxa.

claim: At least 16 of the 22 independent losses of teeth across frogs contain microphagous species.
source: Of the 22 independent losses of teeth across frogs, at least 16 of these lineages contain microphagous species (Figure 4).
evidence: Based on combined ancestral state reconstruction and diet data.

claim: The relative jaw length in frogs ranges from 62% of head length in Synapturanus mirandaribeiroi to 140% of head length in Lepidobatrachus asper.
source: The relative jaw length in frogs ranges from 62% of head length in Synapturanus mirandaribeiroi, an edentulous microhylid, to 140% of head length in Lepidobatrachus asper, a toothed ceratophryid.
evidence: Based on morphometric measurements from 423 anuran species.

claim: A phylogenetic logistic regression showed a significant relationship between edentulism and shortened jaws (p<0.001).
source: A phylogenetic logistic regression showed a significant relationship between edentulism and shortened jaws (alpha = 0.0011, standard error = 0.8920, p<0.001; Figure 5A).
evidence: Result from phylogenetic logistic regression analysis on 423 anuran species.

claim: Edentulous species have an average relative jaw length of 83% of head length.
source: Edentulous species have an average relative jaw length of 83% of head length
evidence: Based on morphometric measurements from 423 anuran species.

claim: Toothed species have an average relative jaw length of 99% of head length.
source: while toothed species have an average relative jaw length of 99% of head length.
evidence: Based on morphometric measurements from 423 anuran species.

claim: The snout–vent length (SVL) of specimens measured ranges from 7.8 mm in the edentulous Paedophryne amauensis to 263.9 mm in the toothed Conraua goliath.
source: The snout–vent length (SVL) of specimens measured ranges from 7.8 mm in the edentulous Paedophryne amauensis, the smallest known frog, to 263.9 mm in the toothed Conraua goliath, the largest known extant species.
evidence: Based on morphometric measurements from 423 anuran species.

claim: A phylogenetic logistic regression indicated that there is no relationship between edentulism and body size (p=0.09).
source: A phylogenetic logistic regression indicated that there is no relationship between edentulism and body size (alpha = 0.0016, standard error = 0.1162, p=0.09; Figure 5B).
evidence: Result from phylogenetic logistic regression analysis on 423 anuran species.

claim: A relationship was found between edentulism and body size when excluding bufonids (p=0.015).
source: However, a relationship was found between edentulism and body size when excluding bufonids (alpha = 0.0020, standard error = 0.1539, p=0.015)
evidence: Result from phylogenetic logistic regression analysis on 377 anuran species (excluding bufonids).

claim: Edentulous species have an average SVL of 36.2 mm (range 7.8–152.4 mm).
source: Edentulous species have an average SVL of 36.2 mm (range 7.8–152.4 mm)
evidence: Based on morphometric measurements from 423 anuran species.

claim: Toothed species have an average SVL of 43.7 mm (range 11.2–263.9 mm).
source: and toothed species have an average SVL of 43.7 (range 11.2–263.9 mm).
evidence: Based on morphometric measurements from 423 anuran species.

claim: Frogs have completely lost teeth more times than any other vertebrate clade.
source: With at least 22 independent origins of edentulism, frogs have completely lost teeth more times than any other vertebrate clade.
evidence: Based on comparison of frog tooth loss data with literature review of other vertebrate groups.

claim: Only eight other extant vertebrate lineages are entirely edentulous.
source: Based on our review of the literature, only eight other extant vertebrate lineages are entirely edentulous.
evidence: Based on literature review of edentulous vertebrate lineages.

claim: There are no described edentulous chondrichthyan species.
source: There are no described edentulous chondrichthyan species (but see Mulas et al., 2020 for the first described aberrant case in a catshark).
evidence: Based on literature review with citation to Mulas et al., 2020.

claim: Teeth have been entirely lost only three times in living actinopterygian fishes in the Gonorynchiformes excluding Gonorynchidae, Gyrinocheilidae, and Syngnathidae.
source: To our knowledge, teeth have been entirely lost only three times in living actinopterygian fishes in the (1) Gonorynchiformes excluding Gonorynchidae (Kohno et al., 1996; Britz and Moritz, 2007), (2) Gyrinocheilidae (Conway, 2011), and (3) Syngnathidae (seahorses and pipefish; Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on literature review with citations to Kohno et al., 1996; Britz and Moritz, 2007; Conway, 2011; Lin et al., 2016.

claim: Five extant amniote clades are edentulous, including three lineages of mammals (baleen whales, pangolins, anteaters), all living birds, and all living turtles.
source: Five extant amniote clades are edentulous, including three lineages of mammals (baleen whales, pangolins, anteaters), all living birds, and all living turtles (Davit-Béal et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on literature review with citation to Davit-Béal et al., 2009.

claim: Molecular evidence suggests a single loss of teeth in the common ancestor of extant birds.
source: Molecular evidence suggests a single loss of teeth in the common ancestor of extant birds (Meredith et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Meredith et al., 2014.

claim: Complete edentulism also evolved independently in at least two extinct lineages of Mesozoic birds (Confuciusornis and Gobipteryx).
source: but complete edentulism also evolved independently in at least two extinct lineages of Mesozoic birds (Confuciusornis and Gobipteryx; Yang and Sander, 2018; Brocklehurst and Field, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang and Sander, 2018; Brocklehurst and Field, 2021.

claim: Teeth were completely lost in at least two lineages of non-avian dinosaurs (ornithomimosaurs and caenagnathoids).
source: Teeth were completely lost in at least two lineages of non-avian dinosaurs (ornithomimosaurs and caenagnathoids; Wang et al., 2017; Hendrickx et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2017; Hendrickx et al., 2019.

claim: At least two fossil suchian archosaurs were edentulous (Shuvosaurus and Effigia).
source: All living crocodilians retain teeth, but at least two fossil suchian archosaurs were edentulous (Shuvosaurus and Effigia; Nesbitt and Norell, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nesbitt and Norell, 2006.

claim: There are no known edentulous squamate species.
source: There are no known edentulous squamate species
evidence: Based on literature review and established knowledge.

claim: African egg-eating snakes in the genus Dasypeltis may have a dental polymorphism, as they typically have small, short teeth but some individuals are reported to be edentulous.
source: although African egg-eating snakes in the genus Dasypeltis may have a dental polymorphism, as they typically have small, short teeth but some individuals are reported to be edentulous (Visser, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citation to Visser, 1981.

claim: The loss of teeth may be associated with the evolution of a secondary feeding apparatus.
source: The loss of teeth may be associated with the evolution of a secondary feeding apparatus (Davit-Béal et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2017)
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations to Davit-Béal et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Nearly all frogs have a specialized tongue that is used in feeding.
source: Nearly all frogs have a specialized tongue that is used in feeding (Regal and Gans, 1976)
evidence: Supported by citation to Regal and Gans, 1976.

claim: The specialized tongue in frogs might have facilitated the repeated loss of teeth across anurans.
source: and this adaptation might have facilitated the repeated loss of teeth across anurans.
evidence: Hypothesis inferred from the presence of specialized tongues and repeated tooth loss.

claim: Three anuran genera are both tongueless and edentulous (Hymenochirus, Pseudhymenochirus, and Pipa in Pipidae).
source: Surprisingly, three anuran genera are both tongueless and edentulous (Hymenochirus, Pseudhymenochirus, and Pipa in Pipidae)
evidence: Based on established knowledge of pipid morphology.

claim: Tongueless and edentulous pipid species are highly aquatic and have a derived mechanism of catching prey under water through suction feeding.
source: but these species are highly aquatic and have a derived mechanism of catching prey under water through suction feeding (Dean, 2003; Cundall et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dean, 2003; Cundall et al., 2017.

claim: There appears to be no size-related constraints promoting complete tooth loss across all vertebrates.
source: There appears to be no size-related constraints promoting complete tooth loss across all vertebrates.
evidence: Inference based on observation that edentulous species span the entire spectrum of vertebrate body sizes.

claim: The smallest known vertebrate species (the microhylid frog P. amauensis) and the largest (the blue whale, Balaenoptera musculus) are both edentulous.
source: Edentulous species span the entire spectrum of vertebrate body sizes: the smallest known vertebrate species (the microhylid frog P. amauensis, Rittmeyer et al., 2012) and the largest (the blue whale, Balaenoptera musculus) are both edentulous.
evidence: Based on established knowledge with citation to Rittmeyer et al., 2012.

claim: Tooth formation occurs ontogenetically late in frogs, during or after metamorphosis, in contrast to during early larval or embryonic development in other vertebrates.
source: Tooth formation occurs ontogenetically late in frogs, during or after metamorphosis, in contrast to during early larval or embryonic development in other vertebrates (Davit-Béal et al., 2007, Lainoff et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davit-Béal et al., 2007, Lainoff et al., 2015.

claim: The delayed shift in odontogenesis may be linked to the evolutionary lability of teeth in anurans.
source: This delayed shift in odontogenesis may be linked to the evolutionary lability of teeth in anurans.
evidence: Hypothesis inferred from the observation of delayed odontogenesis and high frequency of tooth loss.

claim: The dentary bone ossifies relatively late in frogs, and nearly always lacks teeth, compared to being one of the first cranial elements to ossify in salamanders and caecilians.
source: For example, the dentary bone ossifies relatively late in frogs, and nearly always lacks teeth, compared to being one of the first cranial elements to ossify in salamanders and caecilians (Harrington et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Harrington et al., 2013.

claim: Salamanders and caecilians always retain mandibular dentition.
source: and these amphibians always retain mandibular dentition.
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 65 salamander and 30 caecilian species.

claim: Dentition is highly conserved in salamanders and caecilians with no identified cases of edentulism.
source: Dentition is highly conserved in salamanders and caecilians with no identified cases of edentulism.
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 65 salamander and 30 caecilian species.

claim: Teeth are present on the jaws and palate of all caecilians.
source: Teeth are present on the jaws and palate of all caecilians (Wake and Wurst, 1979)
evidence: Based on microCT data and citation to Wake and Wurst, 1979.

claim: The aquatic sirenid salamanders (Siren, Pseudobranchus) lack maxillary and premaxillary teeth.
source: The aquatic sirenid salamanders (Siren, Pseudobranchus) lack maxillary and premaxillary teeth (Clemen and Greven, 1988)
evidence: Based on microCT data and citation to Clemen and Greven, 1988.

claim: The miniaturized species of Thorius sampled (T. pennatulus) lacks maxillary teeth but retains teeth on the premaxilla, palate, and lower jaw.
source: while the miniaturized species of Thorius sampled here (T. pennatulus) lacks maxillary teeth but retains teeth on the premaxilla, palate, and lower jaw.
evidence: Based on microCT examination of T. pennatulus.

claim: At least one species of Thorius possesses a novel dental polymorphism in which males lack maxillary teeth but females maintain several teeth on the maxilla.
source: At least one species of Thorius possesses a novel dental polymorphism in which males lack maxillary teeth but females maintain several teeth on the maxilla (Hanken et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanken et al., 1999.

claim: This is the only known case of a sexually dimorphic presence or absence dental polymorphism in an amphibian.
source: To our knowledge, this is the only known case of a sexually dimorphic presence or absence dental polymorphism in an amphibian.
evidence: Based on literature review and established knowledge.

claim: Maxillary and premaxillary teeth are synchronized in all anuran taxa that we sampled, but two species in the genus Telmatobius have maxillary teeth in the absence of premaxillary teeth.
source: Maxillary and premaxillary teeth are synchronized in all anuran taxa that we sampled, but two species in the genus Telmatobius have maxillary teeth in the absence of premaxillary teeth (Barrionuevo, 2017).
evidence: Based on microCT data and citation to Barrionuevo, 2017.

claim: Two species of Telmatobius are reported to have intraspecific variation in the presence or absence of dentition.
source: Members of this genus can be toothed or edentulous, and two species are reported to have intraspecific variation in the presence or absence of dentition (Barrionuevo, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barrionuevo, 2017.

claim: The loss of vomerine teeth is not a prerequisite for complete tooth loss.
source: The loss of vomerine teeth is not a prerequisite for complete tooth loss (Figure 3)
evidence: Based on discrete character evolution model comparison showing all-rates-different model as best fit.

claim: The presence or absence of teeth on the vomer is not coordinated with dentition on the maxilla and premaxilla in frogs.
source: and the presence or absence of teeth on the vomer is not coordinated with dentition on the maxilla and premaxilla in frogs.
evidence: Based on discrete character evolution model comparison and stochastic character mapping results.

claim: Dentition on the upper jaws and palate are independent modules.
source: These results suggest that dentition on the upper jaws and palate are independent modules
evidence: Inference based on the finding that vomerine tooth loss is not coordinated with maxillary/premaxillary tooth loss.

claim: Teeth are entirely absent in 134 anuran genera distributed across 19 families.
source: Teeth are entirely absent in 134 anuran genera distributed across 19 families
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 429 frog species.

claim: A phylogenetic correlation was identified between the evolution of edentulism and a microphagous diet.
source: We identified a phylogenetic correlation between the evolution of edentulism and a microphagous diet
evidence: Based on BayesTrait discrete analysis showing Bayes factor = 54.32.

claim: Edentulism and microphagy co-occur in more than 50 genera belonging to 14 families.
source: and these two traits co-occur in more than 50 genera belonging to 14 families (Dataset S2; Figure 4).
evidence: Based on combined dentition and diet data for 268 frog lineages.

claim: The majority of edentulous, microphagous frogs specialize on eating ants and termites.
source: The majority of these species specialize on eating ants and termites
evidence: Based on diet data compiled for 268 frog lineages.

claim: Ants and termites have many defense behaviors (biting, stinging, chemical weapons) and low nutritional value compared to other invertebrates.
source: despite that these insects have many defense behaviors (biting, stinging, chemical weapons) and low nutritional value compared to other invertebrates (Redford and Dorea, 1984; McNab, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to Redford and Dorea, 1984; McNab, 1984.

claim: Frogs, ants, and termites evolved at roughly the same time—with important diversification events occurring in all three groups during the Cretaceous and Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary.
source: Frogs, ants, and termites evolved at roughly the same time—with important diversification events occurring in all three groups during the Cretaceous and Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary (Moreau and Bell, 2013; Bourguignon et al., 2015; Feng et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Moreau and Bell, 2013; Bourguignon et al., 2015; Feng et al., 2017.

claim: The repeated evolution of complete edentulism in frogs may be linked to the spatiotemporal diversification of ants and termites.
source: suggesting the repeated evolution of complete edentulism in frogs may be linked to the spatiotemporal diversification of ants and termites.
evidence: Hypothesis inferred from the temporal coincidence of frog, ant, and termite diversification.

claim: Teeth have been repeatedly reduced in other tetrapods that specialize on eating ants and termites, including multiple lineages of mammals and squamates.
source: Teeth have been repeatedly reduced in other tetrapods that specialize on eating ants and termites, including multiple lineages of mammals (echidnas, numbats, aardvarks, aardwolves, anteaters, armadillos, pangolins; Reiss, 2001) and squamates (scolecophidian blind snakes, Aprasia worm lizards; Daza and Bauer, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reiss, 2001; Daza and Bauer, 2015.

claim: The complete loss of teeth in frogs is associated with the shortening of the lower jaw.
source: The complete loss of teeth in frogs is associated with the shortening of the lower jaw (Figure 4)
evidence: Based on phylogenetic logistic regression showing significant relationship (p<0.001).

claim: Shortening of the lower jaw is a skeletal trait that is known to occur in species that eat smaller prey.
source: a skeletal trait that is known to occur in species that eat smaller prey (Emerson, 1985; Vidal-García and Scott Keogh, 2017; Paluh et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Emerson, 1985; Vidal-García and Scott Keogh, 2017; Paluh et al., 2020.

claim: The shortening of the mandible reduces maximum gape and alters jaw biomechanics to improve the efficiency of catching many small prey items.
source: The shortening of the mandible reduces maximum gape and alters jaw biomechanics to improve the efficiency of catching many small prey items.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of jaw biomechanics.

claim: Frogs with a jaw length equal to or longer than the skull have an asymmetrical feeding cycle where the time spent catching prey is short but the time spent bringing prey into the mouth is long.
source: Frogs with a jaw length equal to or longer than the skull have an asymmetrical feeding cycle where the time spent catching prey is short but the time spent bringing prey into the mouth is long (Gans and Gorniak, 1982)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gans and Gorniak, 1982.

claim: Shortened jaws result in a faster, symmetric feeding cycle where equal amounts of time are spent catching and bringing prey into the mouth.
source: shortened jaws result in a faster, symmetric feeding cycle where equal amounts of time are spent catching and bringing prey into the mouth (Emerson, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to Emerson, 1985.

claim: At least four lineages of edentulous anurans that specialize on ants and termites have evolved muscular hydrostatic tongues that can be aimed in all three dimensions and with great precision without moving the head.
source: At least four lineages of edentulous anurans that specialize on ants and termites have additionally evolved muscular hydrostatic tongues that can be aimed in all three dimensions and with great precision without moving the head to improve the efficiency of small prey capture (Rhinophrynus, Trueb and Gans, 1983; Hemisus, Nishikawa et al., 1999; microhylids and brevicipitids, Meyers et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Trueb and Gans, 1983; Nishikawa et al., 1999; Meyers et al., 2004.

claim: Microphagous frogs have been shown to have relatively small eyes among frogs.
source: Recently, these same species have additionally been shown to have relatively small eyes among frogs (Thomas et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2020.

claim: Microphagous frogs may possess improved abilities to process olfactory and tactical cues in order to detect and localize prey.
source: suggesting reduced visual sensitivity and supporting the hypothesis that microphagous frogs may possess improved abilities to process olfactory and tactical cues in order to detect and localize prey (Deban et al., 2001).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citation to Deban et al., 2001.

claim: The evolution of microphagy may have influenced a suite of traits in the head of frogs, including skull shape, jaw position, dentition, tongue morphology, and the functionality of sensory organs.
source: Therefore, the evolution of microphagy may have influenced a suite of traits in the head of frogs, including skull shape, jaw position, dentition, tongue morphology, and the functionality of sensory organs.
evidence: Hypothesis inferred from the multiple correlated traits observed in microphagous frogs.

claim: The majority of the 134 edentulous frogs in the dataset are restricted to the families Bufonidae and Microhylidae.
source: The majority of the 134 edentulous frogs in our dataset are restricted to the families Bufonidae and Microhylidae.
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 429 frog species.

claim: All 48 genera of bufonids examined lack teeth.
source: All 48 genera of bufonids examined—the only anuran clade widely recognized as being edentulous (Davit-Béal et al., 2007)—and 48 of 54 of microhylid genera examined lack teeth.
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 48 bufonid genera with citation to Davit-Béal et al., 2007.

claim: 48 of 54 microhylid genera examined lack teeth.
source: All 48 genera of bufonids examined—the only anuran clade widely recognized as being edentulous (Davit-Béal et al., 2007)—and 48 of 54 of microhylid genera examined lack teeth.
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 54 microhylid genera.

claim: The Bufonidae and Microhylidae are two of the most diverse frog families, comprising 637 and 697 species, respectively (18% of all frogs).
source: The Bufonidae and Microhylidae are two of the most diverse frog families, comprising 637 and 697 species, respectively (18% of all frogs; AmphibiaWeb, 2021).
evidence: Based on taxonomic data from AmphibiaWeb, 2021.

claim: Teeth were independently lost in the most recent common ancestors of both bufonids and microhylids.
source: The results of our ancestral state reconstruction analyses indicate that teeth were independently lost in the most recent common ancestors of both bufonids and microhylids.
evidence: Based on ancestral state reconstruction analysis.

claim: Once lost, teeth have not been regained in the Bufonidae.
source: Once lost, teeth have not been regained in the Bufonidae
evidence: Based on ancestral state reconstruction analysis showing no reversals in Bufonidae.

claim: Teeth may have re-evolved several times in microhylids.
source: but may have re-evolved several times in microhylids.
evidence: Based on ancestral state reconstruction analysis showing six reversals in Microhylidae.

claim: The inferred reversals in Microhylidae occur in Dyscophus, Uperodon, and four cophyline genera (Anodonthyla, Cophyla, Plethodontohyla, Rhombophryne).
source: The inferred reversals in Microhylidae occur in Dyscophus, Uperodon, and four cophyline genera (Anodonthyla, Cophyla, Plethodontohyla, Rhombophryne).
evidence: Based on ancestral state reconstruction analysis.

claim: If teeth were entirely lost in the common ancestor of microhylids, the repeated re-evolution of true teeth (with enamel, dentin, and pulp cavity) in this clade is unlikely and requires histological investigation.
source: If teeth were entirely lost in the common ancestor of microhylids, the repeated re-evolution of true teeth (with enamel, dentin, and pulp cavity) in this clade is unlikely and requires histological investigation.
evidence: Speculation based on the improbability of re-evolving complex structures.

claim: The tooth-like structures in some microhylid taxa may be small odontoids (bony serrations that lack the tissue composition of true teeth).
source: We hypothesize the tooth-like structures in some of these taxa, such as Rhombophryne and Uperodon (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), may be small odontoids (bony serrations that lack the tissue composition of true teeth; Fabrezi and Emerson, 2003)
evidence: Hypothesis based on comparison with similar structures described in other taxa, supported by citation to Fabrezi and Emerson, 2003.

claim: The dental anatomy of Dyscophus has been examined and this genus does possess true teeth.
source: The dental anatomy of Dyscophus has been examined (LaDouceur et al., 2020), and this genus does possess true teeth.
evidence: Supported by citation to LaDouceur et al., 2020.

claim: The morphology of Dyscophus, Anodonthyla, Cophyla, and Plethodontohyla indicates that these taxa have true dentition based on the presence of replacement teeth and/or floating teeth that are undergoing resorption.
source: The morphology of Dyscophus, Anodonthyla, Cophyla, and Plethodontohyla indicates that these taxa have true dentition based on the presence of replacement teeth and/or floating teeth that are undergoing resorption (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on microCT examination showing replacement teeth and resorption patterns.

claim: Of the ten anuran genera known to possess variation in the presence or absence of teeth, diet data are only available for Physalaemus and Engystomops.
source: Of the ten anuran genera known to possess variation in the presence or absence of teeth, diet data are only available for Physalaemus and Engystomops.
evidence: Based on literature review of diet data.

claim: In both Physalaemus and Engystomops, edentulous species have specialized microphagous diets in comparison to toothed congeners that consume a broader array of invertebrates.
source: In both genera, edentulous species have specialized microphagous diets in comparison to toothed congeners that consume a broader array of invertebrates (Narváez and Ron, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Narváez and Ron, 2013.

claim: Dietary alkaloid sequestration has evolved as a predator defense mechanism in at least five clades of frogs that specialize on eating ants and mites.
source: Dietary alkaloid sequestration has evolved as a predator defense mechanism in at least five clades of frogs that specialize on eating ants and mites
evidence: Based on established knowledge and citations provided.

claim: Teeth have been lost in several lineages that sequester dietary alkaloids.
source: and teeth have been lost in several of these lineages (Dendrobatinae and Ameerega [Dendrobatidae, Saporito et al., 2004]; Pseudophryne [Myobatrachidae, Smith et al., 2002]; Mantella [Mantellidae, Daly et al., 1997]; Melanophryniscus [Bufonidae, Hantak et al., 2013]).
evidence: Supported by citations to Saporito et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2002; Daly et al., 1997; Hantak et al., 2013.

claim: No relationship was identified between complete edentulism and body size in the 423 frog species sampled.
source: No relationship was identified between complete edentulism and body size in the 423 frog species sampled.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic logistic regression showing p=0.09.

claim: The smallest known species of frog, P. amauensis, lacks teeth.
source: The smallest known species of frog, P. amauensis, lacks teeth
evidence: Based on microCT examination.

claim: Some miniaturized anurans are toothed.
source: but some miniaturized anurans are toothed.
evidence: Based on microCT examination of 423 frog species.

claim: Of 25 taxa with an SVL of 15 mm or less, 13 were toothed and 12 were edentulous.
source: We examined 25 taxa with an SVL of 15 mm or less: 13 were toothed and 12 were edentulous.
evidence: Based on morphometric measurements from 423 anuran species.

claim: When excluding bufonids, reduction in body size was phylogenetically correlated with edentulism.
source: When excluding bufonids, reduction in body size was phylogenetically correlated with edentulism
evidence: Based on phylogenetic logistic regression showing p=0.015 when excluding bufonids.

claim: No stem tetrapods have been described as edentulous.
source: To our knowledge, no stem tetrapods have been described as edentulous (Ruta et al., 2003; Anderson et al., 2008; Matsumoto and Evans, 2017).
evidence: Based on literature review with citations to Ruta et al., 2003; Anderson et al., 2008; Matsumoto and Evans, 2017.

claim: Albanerpetontids, an extinct lineage of lissamphibians, had teeth on the premaxilla, maxilla, and dentary.
source: Albanerpetontids, an extinct lineage of lissamphibians, had teeth on the premaxilla, maxilla, and dentary (Daza et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Daza et al., 2020.

claim: There is no evidence of edentulism in fossil salamanders or caecilians.
source: and there is no evidence of edentulism in fossil salamanders or caecilians.
evidence: Based on literature review.

claim: Teeth are present on the upper jaw in the stem salientians Prosalirus, Vieraella, and Liaobatrachus.
source: Of the stem salientians with cranial material, teeth are present on the upper jaw in Prosalirus (Shubin and Jenkins, 1995), Vieraella (Báez and Basso, 1996), and Liaobatrachus (Gao and Wang, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shubin and Jenkins, 1995; Báez and Basso, 1996; Gao and Wang, 2001.

claim: No teeth are visible in Triadobatrachus, but the maxilla and premaxilla are poorly preserved in this impression fossil.
source: No teeth are visible in Triadobatrachus (Ascarrunz et al., 2016), the oldest known stem frog, but the maxilla and premaxilla are poorly preserved in this impression fossil.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ascarrunz et al., 2016.

claim: The dentary of Triadobatrachus lacks teeth, and the absence of dentition on the lower jaw is considered a synapomorphy of Salientia.
source: The dentary of Triadobatrachus lacks teeth, and the absence of dentition on the lower jaw is considered a synapomorphy of Salientia (Milner, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to Milner, 1988.

claim: Several extinct crown-group anuran genera are edentulous, and the majority of these are hypothesized to be members of the Pipidae.
source: Several extinct crown-group anuran genera are edentulous, and the majority of these are hypothesized to be members of the Pipidae (Báez and Harrison, 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Báez and Harrison, 2005.

claim: Extinct edentulous pipids likely represent two or more instances of tooth loss.
source: Based on the phylogenetic analyses of Báez and Harrison, 2005 and Trueb et al., 2005, extinct edentulous pipids likely represent two or more instances of tooth loss
evidence: Inference based on phylogenetic analyses cited.

claim: The clades Xenopodinomorpha and Pipinomorpha are not supported by molecular phylogenetic analyses of living pipids.
source: However, the clades Xenopodinomorpha and Pipinomorpha are not supported by molecular phylogenetic analyses of living pipids (Irisarri et al., 2011; Feng et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Irisarri et al., 2011; Feng et al., 2017.

claim: Tooth loss likely occurred in pipids at earliest during the mid-Cretaceous because all described pipimorph frogs from the early Cretaceous are toothed.
source: Tooth loss likely occurred in pipids at earliest during the mid-Cretaceous because all described pipimorph frogs from the early Cretaceous are toothed (Báez et al., 2021): Thoraciliacus (Trueb, 1999), Cordicephalus (Trueb and Báez, 2006), Neusibatrachus, and Gracilibatrachus (Báez, 2013).
evidence: Inference based on fossil record with citations to Báez et al., 2021; Trueb, 1999; Trueb and Báez, 2006; Báez, 2013.

claim: Ancestral state reconstructions suggest that living pipid frogs have lost teeth twice independently in the ancestor of Hymenochirus + Pseudhymenochirus and in Pipa.
source: Our ancestral state reconstructions suggest that living pipid frogs have lost teeth twice independently in the ancestor of Hymenochirus + Pseudhymenochirus and in Pipa (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on ancestral state reconstruction analysis.

claim: All species of Xenopus and three of seven species of Pipa have teeth (P. carvalhoi, P. aspera, P. arrabali).
source: All species of Xenopus and three of seven species of Pipa have teeth (P. carvalhoi, P. aspera, P. arrabali; Trueb and Cannatella, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Trueb and Cannatella, 1986.

claim: The fossil record of Rhinophrynidae includes the toothed Rhadinosteus from the late Jurassic of Utah and the edentulous Chelomophrynus from the Eocene of Wyoming.
source: The fossil record of Rhinophrynidae is sparse (Blackburn et al., 2019) but includes the toothed Rhadinosteus from the late Jurassic of Utah (Henrici, 1998) and the edentulous Chelomophrynus from the Eocene of Wyoming (Henrici, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blackburn et al., 2019; Henrici, 1998; Henrici, 1991.

claim: The presence of teeth in Rhadinosteus supports the hypothesis that teeth were lost independently in pipids and rhinophrynids.
source: The presence of teeth in Rhadinosteus supports the hypothesis that teeth were lost independently in pipids and rhinophrynids (Figure 2)
evidence: Inference based on fossil evidence and ancestral state reconstruction.

claim: Two edentulous, non-pipoid fossil frogs have been described from the Mesozoic of the Northern Hemisphere: Theatonius from the late Cretaceous of Wyoming and Tyrrellbatrachus from the late Cretaceous of Alberta.
source: Two edentulous, non-pipoid fossil frogs have been described from the Mesozoic of the Northern Hemisphere: Theatonius from the late Cretaceous of Wyoming (Fox, 1976) and Tyrrellbatrachus from the late Cretaceous of Alberta (Gardner, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fox, 1976; Gardner, 2015.

claim: Theatonius and Tyrrellbatrachus likely represent two independent cases of tooth loss and possibly the oldest record of edentulism in nonpipid frogs.
source: Gardner, 2015 hypothesized that these two taxa likely represent two independent cases of tooth loss and possibly the oldest record of edentulism in nonpipid frogs.
evidence: Hypothesis from Gardner, 2015.

claim: Several lineages of edentulous vertebrates have various states of molecular tooth decay in the genes that are critical for the formation of dentin and enamel with frameshift mutations and stop codons that result in nonfunctionalization.
source: Recent work has documented that several lineages of edentulous vertebrates have various states of molecular tooth decay in the genes that are critical for the formation of dentin and enamel with frameshift mutations and stop codons that result in nonfunctionalization (mammals: Meredith et al., 2009; turtles: Meredith et al., 2013; birds: Meredith et al., 2014; syngnathids: Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meredith et al., 2009; Meredith et al., 2013; Meredith et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2016.

claim: Lu et al., 2021 failed to identify any dentin or enamel genes in the genomes of two bufonids (R. marina and B. gargarizans).
source: Recently, Lu et al., 2021 failed to identify any dentin or enamel genes in the genomes of two bufonids (R. marina and B. gargarizans)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2021.

claim: Shaheen et al., 2021 demonstrated pseudogenization of the major tooth enamel gene amelogenin in R. marina, B. gargarizans, and B. bufo.
source: but Shaheen et al., 2021 demonstrated pseudogenization of the major tooth enamel gene amelogenin in R. marina, B. gargarizans, and B. bufo.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shaheen et al., 2021.

claim: The amelogenin gene likely became inactivated in the Bufonidae 40–60 million years ago.
source: Based on selection intensity estimates and substitution rates, this gene likely became inactivated in the Bufonidae 40–60 million years ago (Shaheen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shaheen et al., 2021.

claim: Tooth-specific genes have degenerated repeatedly across edentulous anurans by novel inactivating mutations.
source: We hypothesize that these tooth-specific genes have degenerated repeatedly across edentulous anurans by novel inactivating mutations
evidence: Hypothesis based on patterns observed in other edentulous vertebrates.

claim: The developmental genetics of tooth formation in amphibians is almost entirely unexplored.
source: The developmental genetics of tooth formation in amphibians is almost entirely unexplored, especially when compared to our understanding of chondrichthyan, teleost, and amniote odontogenesis (Fraser et al., 2004; Tucker and Sharpe, 2004; Thiery et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on literature review with citations to Fraser et al., 2004; Tucker and Sharpe, 2004; Thiery et al., 2017.
